cultivar: Yueyang local landrace and Fuding Dabai
processing: A bud with one or two leaves is pan-fired, piled briefly to yellow while warm, lightly rolled, then dried in stages; a light yellowing in the 'yellow small tea' style.
harvest_season: Spring, from late March to late April; pre-Qingming and yu qian lots.
appearance_dry: Slightly curled, downy shoots in yellow-green with golden tips.
appearance_wet: Tender yellow-green bud-and-leaf sets, even and soft.
taste_profile: Mellow and sweet with chestnut and a light floral note, a soft round body and a clean, gentle finish.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan or glass at 80–85 °C. A gentle bud tea; four steeps, with the first two carrying most of the flavour.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest in pre-Qingming and yu qian lots, mostly within Hunan and at a fraction of the price of Junshan Yinzhen, its island neighbour. A good deal of Beigang-area bud tea is sold under the Junshan name instead. Drink within the year, kept cold and sealed.
description:
Beigang Mao Jian is the yellow tea of the mainland shore opposite Junshan Island, from the Beigang district of Yueyang in Hunan on the edge of Dongting Lake. It belongs to the 'yellow small tea' group, bud-with-leaf teas given a light yellowing, and it is the honest, affordable cousin of the island's famous Silver Needle.

The leaf is pan-fired, then piled briefly while still warm so it yellows a little, rolled lightly and dried in stages. The yellowing is short compared with Junshan's three days, so the tea sits closer to a mellow green than to a fully yellowed bud tea, with a golden tint rather than a golden colour.

In the cup it is mellow and sweet, chestnut and a light floral note, a soft round body and a clean gentle finish, with the grassy edge of a green bud tea sanded off. It takes 80–85 °C in a gaiwan and gives four steeps. It is not a dramatic tea; it is a pleasant daily one.

It is sold as the spring crop of the current year in pre-Qingming and yu qian lots, almost entirely within Hunan, and it is cheap. The irony of the Beigang name is that a good deal of the area's bud tea goes out dressed as Junshan Yinzhen instead; bought honestly under its own name it is good value. Check for a yellow-green rather than green leaf and a mellow rather than grassy smell.

If you have been burned by an expensive 'Junshan' that tasted like green tea, this is probably what you drank, and it is worth having for what it is.
